messages.content: I want to develop a learned surrogate for compressible Euler dynamics that preserves conservation and entropy admissibility across shocks on unseen meshes. The quantitative conservation requirement is to keep normalized mass, momentum, and energy drift below 10⁻⁶ over 1,000 periodic, unforced timesteps. It also needs to match an entropy-stable finite-volume baseline’s shock accuracy without increasing discrete entropy violations on unseen meshes.

That sets two requirements for the surrogate. Its long-time evolution must keep each named conserved quantity—mass, momentum, and energy—within the stated normalized drift limit under the specified periodic, unforced conditions. At shocks, it must retain the entropy-stable finite-volume baseline’s accuracy while not increasing discrete entropy violations on unseen meshes. These are goals for the model, not results already established.
When I say conservation, do you read that as one aggregate score for all three quantities?

No. The wording names mass, momentum, and energy individually, so an aggregate score would not, by itself, show that each meets the below-10⁻⁶ normalized drift requirement. Momentum may have multiple components; how those components are assessed would need to be specified when the requirement is made operational. I would not silently let a small error in one quantity compensate for a larger error in another.
And the 1,000 timesteps are part of the condition, not just background context?

Yes. The stated limit is for 1,000 periodic, unforced timesteps. A result from a shorter evolution, or from different boundary or forcing conditions, would not establish that particular requirement. The phrase “over 1,000” also points to behavior during the evolution, rather than inviting an assumption that only a favorable final value matters; the exact way drift is assessed across the interval would need to be defined.
Why does the periodic, unforced qualification matter to the conservation statement?

It identifies the setting in which that drift target applies. In a periodic, unforced evolution, the conservation question is not being framed around prescribed inflow, outflow, or an external forcing contribution. That makes the requirement more precise without extending the below-10⁻⁶ target to settings the goal does not mention.
Does “normalized drift” already tell us exactly how to calculate the number?

Not on its own. It says the drift is measured on a normalized scale, but it does not specify the normalization, how a momentum vector is handled, or how values across timesteps are combined. Those choices matter for interpreting a threshold as small as 10⁻⁶. They should be stated for an assessment, rather than treated as details the goal has already fixed.
I also want “across shocks” to have real force here. Is conservation alone enough to cover it?

No. Conservation addresses whether the evolution respects the relevant balances; entropy admissibility addresses whether shock behavior satisfies the appropriate entropy condition. A surrogate could be judged on conservation and still need a separate assessment of its shock behavior and discrete entropy violations. The goal explicitly asks for both.
Can you clarify entropy admissibility without assuming that entropy must stay exactly constant through a shock?

Exactly constant entropy through a shock is not the intended reading. Entropy admissibility distinguishes physically appropriate shock behavior from behavior that would violate the applicable entropy condition. At the discrete level, the requirement is concerned with violations of that condition, not with demanding entropy equality across shocks. The sign convention and precise discrete test have not been specified here.
What is the baseline doing in the shock requirement?

The entropy-stable finite-volume baseline is the named comparator for shock accuracy. The surrogate is required to match its shock accuracy, while also meeting the condition about discrete entropy violations on unseen meshes. The statement does not give a particular shock-error metric or a measured baseline value, so it would be premature to claim a numerical match.
Could better shock accuracy make an increase in discrete entropy violations acceptable?

Not under this wording. Matching the baseline’s shock accuracy and avoiding an increase in discrete entropy violations are joined requirements, not a proposed tradeoff. Improved performance on one aspect would not erase a failure on the other. The goal does not prescribe an exchange rate between accuracy and admissibility.
How should we understand “unseen meshes” without inventing a particular mesh test?

It means the shock-accuracy and discrete-entropy expectations must hold beyond meshes already seen by the learned surrogate. The goal does not identify mesh families, resolutions, or a testing split, so none should be presumed. Its substantive point is that success on familiar meshes alone is not enough to establish the stated shock behavior.
Does the unseen-mesh condition also modify the 1,000-timestep drift threshold?

The conservation requirement explicitly specifies the below-10⁻⁶ normalized drift threshold over 1,000 periodic, unforced timesteps. The shock-accuracy and discrete-entropy requirement explicitly mentions unseen meshes. The overall goal also calls for conservation and entropy admissibility across shocks on unseen meshes, but the wording does not spell out a separate mesh-specific conservation test. I would preserve those stated conditions rather than invent an additional protocol.
Is “match shock accuracy” the same as saying the surrogate has to reproduce the baseline’s predictions everywhere?

No. It is a comparison of shock accuracy, not a demand for identical predictions at every point or in every state. Accuracy near a shock can be discussed in terms of how well the shock is represented, but this goal has not selected a particular measure. Whatever comparison is eventually used should address the stated shock-accuracy requirement rather than quietly replacing it with overall prediction similarity.
Could we describe a successful model as one with low average conservation error and generally reasonable-looking shocks?

That description would be too weak. An average could conceal drift above 10⁻⁶ for one of mass, momentum, or energy, and “reasonable-looking” does not establish a match to the entropy-stable finite-volume baseline’s shock accuracy. It also says nothing definite about discrete entropy violations on unseen meshes. The specific conditions are what make this goal testable.
What should we avoid claiming while we discuss this as a development goal?

We should avoid saying the surrogate already meets the threshold, already matches the baseline, or has demonstrated entropy admissibility on unseen meshes. We should also avoid supplying an unstated normalization, entropy-violation measure, shock metric, mesh collection, or implementation as though one had been chosen. Those details may matter to an eventual evaluation, but they are not results or decisions contained in the goal.

Let me check my wording: the learned surrogate is for compressible Euler dynamics; mass, momentum, and energy must each remain under 10⁻⁶ normalized drift over 1,000 periodic, unforced timesteps; and on unseen meshes its shock accuracy must match an entropy-stable finite-volume baseline without increased discrete entropy violations. Is that faithful?

Yes. That retains the dynamics, all three conserved quantities, the numerical threshold and timestep conditions, the named shock-accuracy comparator, and the unseen-mesh entropy constraint. I would keep the broader aim explicit as well: preservation of conservation and entropy admissibility across shocks on unseen meshes.

For the learned surrogate, I propose learning mesh-equivariant, positive-semidefinite entropy-variable dissipation around entropy-conservative face fluxes, with shared face updates and timestep entropy limiting. Can we unpack how those pieces fit together?

Yes. The entropy-conservative face fluxes provide the proposed starting point for interactions between neighboring states. The learned component supplies dissipation expressed through entropy variables, with a positive-semidefinite structure so its contribution has the intended dissipative sign. Mesh equivariance concerns how that component behaves when a mesh is represented differently. Shared face updates address conservation across a face, while timestep entropy limiting addresses admissibility of the completed time update. This is a proposed design, not a demonstrated result.
Does “learn dissipation around entropy-conservative face fluxes” mean learning the whole flux from scratch?

No. In this proposal, the entropy-conservative face flux remains an identifiable part of the face interaction. What is learned is the dissipative contribution around it. That distinction matters: it describes where learning enters without claiming that the learned component replaces the entropy-conservative flux or that its behavior has already been validated.
Why express the dissipation in entropy variables rather than just calling it a correction to the flux?

Calling it a correction would leave its admissibility structure unclear. Entropy variables let the proposal tie the dissipative contribution to an entropy argument: with an appropriate positive-semidefinite operator acting on their jump, the relevant quadratic contribution has a nonnegative dissipative magnitude under the chosen sign convention. The precise entropy, scaling, and flux construction have not been specified, so that is a structural explanation rather than a claim about a particular implementation.
When you say positive semidefinite, is every entry of the learned object required to be positive?

No. Positive semidefiniteness is a property of a quadratic form, not a requirement that every entry be positive. In the usual matrix interpretation, it means that the quadratic form is nonnegative for every vector to which it applies. Here, the relevant vectors are associated with differences in entropy variables. The proposal does not specify how that property would be imposed in a learned parameterization.
Does positive-semidefinite entropy-variable dissipation automatically make the entire surrogate entropy admissible?

It supplies an important structural ingredient, but it does not by itself settle every part of the claim. An entropy-conservative base flux combined with dissipative terms of the appropriate sign can support a discrete entropy argument at the face or semidiscrete level, subject to the flux and discretization assumptions. A completed timestep can raise a separate entropy question, which is why the proposal also includes timestep entropy limiting. None of that establishes admissibility on unseen meshes without evaluation.
So the timestep entropy limiter is not merely another name for the positive-semidefinite dissipation?

Right. They operate at different points in the proposed reasoning. The learned dissipation structures the face contribution; timestep entropy limiting is meant to constrain the entropy behavior of an update after time advancement is taken into account. The proposal names that limiting step but does not prescribe its formula, activation rule, or effect on accuracy.
What does “shared face updates” mean for two neighboring cells?

The face interaction is shared by the cells on its two sides, rather than each cell receiving an independently predicted interface contribution. In a conservative update, the contribution assigned through their common face is accounted for with opposing orientations. That makes the face contribution cancel when the two cell balances are combined. The proposal does not specify a storage scheme or an algorithm for assembling those updates.
Is that sharing particularly relevant to conservation?

Yes. If neighboring cells used unrelated predictions for what crosses their common face, cancellation would not follow from the face construction. Sharing the face interaction is the proposed structural way to make their accounting consistent. It supports conservation by design, but it is not, on its own, a measured statement about long-time drift or every other part of an update.
I want to be precise about mesh equivariance. Is it the same as giving the model information about mesh geometry?

Not exactly. Mesh equivariance is about consistent behavior under a change in how the same mesh and its associated states are represented—for example, a consistent relabeling should correspondingly relabel the output, not change the underlying physical update. Geometry may matter to a face interaction, but simply providing geometric information does not establish equivariance. The proposal does not choose a specific representation or enumerate every transformation it will handle.
If I reverse which neighboring cell I call the first one, should that change the physical face exchange?

A consistent reversal of face orientation should change the oriented description consistently, not produce an unrelated physical exchange. That is a useful way to understand the combination of mesh-equivariant behavior and a shared face update. The exact transformation rules for the learned dissipation and flux would have to be specified in an implementation; they are not fixed by this proposal alone.
How do the four components relate to shocks?

The dissipative contribution is the part of this proposal intended to handle behavior for which an entropy-conservative flux alone is not the whole admissibility story, including shocks. Its positive-semidefinite entropy-variable structure is intended to keep that contribution compatible with entropy dissipation. Sharing the face update preserves consistent exchange across the interface, and timestep entropy limiting addresses the completed update. The proposal does not assert that these choices already achieve a particular shock accuracy.
Could I say the limiter will always fix any entropy problem, regardless of the learned dissipation?

That would overstate the proposal. It calls for timestep entropy limiting, but does not specify a limiter or prove that it can correct every possible issue while preserving the desired update. The proposed pieces are meant to work together; the presence of a limiter is not a blanket guarantee of entropy admissibility or shock accuracy.
Does mesh equivariance itself guarantee that the approach works on unseen meshes?

No. Equivariance can prevent changes in representation from spuriously changing the model’s behavior, which is valuable when working with meshes. It does not guarantee accurate or entropy-admissible dynamics on meshes the surrogate has not encountered. Those outcomes would still need to be assessed; the proposal specifies a structural approach, not an established generalization result.
Could the learned dissipation be described as unrestricted as long as a timestep limiter follows it?

No. Positive semidefiniteness in entropy variables is an explicit constraint on the learned dissipation itself. The timestep limiter is an additional component, not permission to discard that structure. Likewise, the learned contribution is positioned around entropy-conservative face fluxes and used with shared face updates; those are parts of the proposal, not optional details implied by the limiter.
And should we name a particular neural architecture or limiter formula when stating the proposal?

Not unless one is separately specified. “Learned” identifies what is being fitted, while “mesh-equivariant” and “positive-semidefinite” identify intended structural properties. The current proposal does not choose an architecture, a way to parameterize the dissipative operator, or a timestep-limiting formula. Adding one would turn an explanation of the proposal into an unsupported design decision.

Let me try a compact formulation: retain entropy-conservative fluxes at faces, learn a mesh-equivariant positive-semidefinite dissipative term in entropy variables, apply each face interaction as a shared update, and limit the timestep for entropy. Does that preserve the proposal?

Yes. I would say “timestep entropy limiting” to make clear what the limiting is intended to address. Your formulation otherwise keeps the proposed division of roles intact: an entropy-conservative face-flux foundation, structured learned dissipation, shared accounting at faces, and an entropy constraint on the timestep update. It remains a proposed construction rather than a claim that its conservation, entropy, or shock-accuracy goals have been met.

Here is the question I want to resolve: can learned face dissipation retain the entropy-stable finite-volume baseline’s shock-position accuracy on unseen meshes while the entropy limiter prevents discrete entropy increases?

That is the key joint question for the proposed construction. The learned face dissipation would need to represent shocks well enough to retain the baseline’s shock-position accuracy on unseen meshes, and the timestep entropy limiter would need to prevent discrete entropy increases. Neither outcome, nor their coexistence, has been established by the proposal alone.
Why ask about both at once rather than checking shock position and entropy separately?

Because they concern the same completed evolution. Learned dissipation may affect how a shock is represented and where it moves; entropy limiting may also affect the update used to advance it. Showing that one component has a desirable property in isolation would not answer whether the resulting limited surrogate retains shock-position accuracy while preventing discrete entropy increases.
Is shock-position accuracy narrower than the shock accuracy in the overall goal?

Yes. Shock-position accuracy concerns where the shock is represented. The broader phrase “shock accuracy” need not be limited to position alone. This question focuses on whether position accuracy can be retained relative to the named baseline; answering it would not automatically settle every aspect of shock accuracy.
When I say “retain baseline shock-position accuracy,” am I claiming the learned model already matches it?

No. You are asking whether it can do so. The entropy-stable finite-volume baseline is the comparator, but the question supplies no measured shock positions or errors for either approach. It should remain an open comparison, especially on unseen meshes.
What work is “unseen meshes” doing in this question?

It requires the shock-position comparison to extend beyond meshes the learned dissipation has already encountered. Accurate shock placement on a familiar mesh would not, by itself, answer the question. Nothing here specifies which unseen meshes or how their shock positions would be measured, so those details should not be assumed.
Is positive-semidefinite entropy-variable dissipation enough to answer the entropy half?

Not by itself. That structure is intended to give the face dissipation an appropriate entropy sign, but the question asks whether the entropy limiter prevents discrete entropy increases in the completed update. A structural property of the face term should not be treated as a result about every timestep after limiting.
And does an entropy limiter necessarily leave shock position unchanged?

No such guarantee is stated. Limiting constrains the update for entropy reasons, and a changed update could also change the represented shock position. That possibility is why retaining baseline shock-position accuracy and preventing discrete entropy increases are a joint question rather than two outcomes we can assume are independent.
Could sufficiently accurate learned dissipation compensate for whatever the limiter does?

It is possible to ask whether the components can work together that way, but the question does not establish that compensation occurs. Nor does it say how frequently limiting would matter or how it would affect shock motion. Those would be properties of a particular surrogate and its behavior, not facts supplied here.
Should “prevents discrete entropy increases” be read as a claim that physical entropy never increases at shocks?

No. The phrase concerns a discrete entropy condition for the numerical update, under the relevant entropy convention. It should not be turned into a blanket statement that physical entropy is constant or cannot increase across a shock. The particular discrete entropy quantity and sign convention would need to be stated to interpret a numerical check precisely.
Could we call the question answered if the limiter prevents increases but shock position is worse than the baseline’s?

Not affirmatively. Preventing discrete entropy increases would address one clause, but the question also asks whether the surrogate retains the baseline’s shock-position accuracy on unseen meshes. A loss of that accuracy would mean the proposed combination had not achieved both requested properties in that comparison.
What if shock position matches the baseline, but discrete entropy still increases?

That would likewise leave the joint question unanswered in the affirmative. Matching shock position would not show that the entropy limiter prevents discrete entropy increases. The two conditions are simultaneous; neither is a substitute for the other.
Does the word “prevents” allow occasional increases as long as there are fewer than in the baseline?

Not in this question. “Prevents discrete entropy increases” asks for no such increases under the intended discrete entropy test. That is distinct in wording from the broader goal’s comparison about not increasing discrete entropy violations relative to the baseline on unseen meshes. We should not silently replace the absolute wording here with a relative count.
Does mesh equivariance decide whether the shock-position comparison will succeed?

No. Mesh equivariance is a proposed consistency property of the learned dissipation under changes in mesh representation. It does not establish how accurately shocks will be positioned on unseen meshes. The question remains about the behavior of the learned dissipation together with the entropy-limited update.
Can shared face updates resolve the question on their own?

No. Shared face updates support consistent accounting across neighboring cells, which is relevant to conservation. They do not by themselves demonstrate baseline shock-position accuracy or show that the timestep limiter prevents discrete entropy increases. They remain part of the proposed construction, but the two outcomes in this question require their own assessment.
What would an answer have to distinguish to avoid being misleading?

It would have to distinguish shock-position accuracy from broader shock accuracy, the unseen-mesh comparison from behavior on familiar meshes, and the entropy behavior of a face contribution from that of the completed timestep. Most importantly, it would have to address both the baseline comparison and the prevention of discrete entropy increases, rather than inferring either one solely from the proposed structure.
So for now the careful statement is that the learned face dissipation and entropy limiter are intended to achieve those properties together, but whether they actually do on unseen meshes is open?

Yes. The question is whether learned face dissipation can retain the entropy-stable finite-volume baseline’s shock-position accuracy on unseen meshes while the timestep entropy limiter prevents discrete entropy increases. The proposed structure motivates asking it; it does not yet supply the answer.
My hypothesis is that, on unseen meshes, learned fluxes will achieve density L1 error within 5% of the baseline and zero positive global entropy residuals.

That is a prediction, not an observed result. It has two parts on unseen meshes: the learned fluxes’ density L1 error will be within 5% of the baseline’s, and the assessed global entropy residuals will include no positive values. Both parts would need to hold for the hypothesis as stated.
Is the 5% about density error, rather than a 5% difference in the density values themselves?

Yes. The comparison is between density L1 errors. It does not say that predicted density values at every location are within 5% of baseline density values. An L1 error summarizes absolute density discrepancies under some reference and weighting convention, neither of which is specified in the hypothesis.
Does “within 5% of baseline” identify a fixed numerical L1-error threshold?

No. It gives a relative comparison with the baseline’s density L1 error, not an absolute error value. Interpreting it numerically would require the baseline error and an explicit convention for calculating the percentage difference, particularly if the baseline error were zero. The hypothesis supplies neither a measured baseline value nor that convention.
Could we just restate it as “no worse than 1.05 times the baseline error”?

That captures a common upper-bound interpretation, but it is not necessarily identical to “within 5%,” which can also be read as a two-sided closeness criterion. I would retain the original wording unless you intend to specify one interpretation. Either way, the comparison concerns density L1 error, not a claim of identical density fields.
Does this directly answer our question about shock-position accuracy?

Not directly. The hypothesis gives a density L1-error comparison, whereas shock-position accuracy is a more specific property. Density L1 error may reflect discrepancies associated with shocks, but meeting the within-5% comparison would not, by itself, establish that shock positions match the baseline’s accuracy. The entropy-residual part likewise needs to be read on its own terms.
But the hypothesis is related to that question, correct?

Yes. It offers predicted outcomes for the learned fluxes on unseen meshes that speak to accuracy and entropy behavior. Its stated accuracy measure is density L1 error, and its stated entropy measure is positive global entropy residuals. Those measures do not silently become a shock-position metric or every possible discrete entropy test.
What exactly does “zero positive global entropy residuals” assert?

It asserts that none of the global entropy residuals considered in the assessment will be positive. Zero-valued residuals would not be positive, and neither would negative ones. The hypothesis does not specify how a residual is computed, how many updates or cases are assessed, or what numerical tolerance is used to classify its sign.
Is that equivalent to saying the global entropy residual is exactly zero every time?

No. “Zero positive global entropy residuals” counts positive residuals; it does not require each residual to equal zero. A nonpositive residual would satisfy the sign statement. Treating it as an exact-equality requirement would change the hypothesis.
Does it say that no cell or face ever has a positive entropy residual?

No. The qualifier is “global.” A global residual concerns an aggregate entropy assessment, and its nonpositivity does not automatically establish the sign of every local cell or face contribution. The hypothesis does not make a separate claim about local residuals.
Should we assume a particular physical entropy sign convention when we read “positive”?

We should not supply an unstated formula or sign convention. The hypothesis identifies positive global entropy residuals as the outcomes it predicts will be absent. To evaluate that prediction consistently, the residual’s definition and sign would have to be fixed; the wording alone does not provide them.
Does “on unseen meshes” apply to just the density L1 comparison, or to both predictions?

It applies to the hypothesis as a whole: the density L1-error comparison and the absence of positive global entropy residuals are both predicted on unseen meshes. The statement does not specify which meshes, how many there are, or how results across them are aggregated.
Could a good average across unseen meshes establish the hypothesis if one mesh has a positive global entropy residual?

An average alone would not establish “zero positive global entropy residuals” if the assessed set contains a positive one. For the density L1 comparison, the hypothesis has not specified whether “within 5%” is evaluated mesh by mesh or through an aggregate, so that aspect would need clarification before interpreting an average. We should not let averaging silently weaken the explicit zero-positive condition.
Does the hypothesis claim that the entropy limiter is what causes the predicted entropy result?

No. It predicts an outcome for learned fluxes, not a causal finding about which component produces it. The earlier proposed construction includes timestep entropy limiting, but this hypothesis does not report an experiment isolating its effect or assert that the limiter alone guarantees zero positive global entropy residuals.
What about conservation—does zero positive global entropy residuals imply the long-time mass, momentum, and energy target?

No. Entropy-residual sign and conservation drift are different assessments. This hypothesis does not state a mass, momentum, or energy drift result. Its two specified predictions are the density L1-error comparison and zero positive global entropy residuals on unseen meshes.
Can I describe the density result as matching the baseline’s shock accuracy?

That would be broader than the hypothesis. Density L1 error within 5% of baseline is a particular accuracy comparison; it is not explicitly a comparison of shock position or all aspects of shock accuracy. It is more precise to name the density L1 measure rather than substitute a different metric.
And can I call the entropy result a proof of entropy admissibility everywhere?

Not from this hypothesis. It predicts an absence of positive *global* entropy residuals on unseen meshes under an as-yet-unspecified assessment. It neither reports that outcome nor makes a claim about every local entropy measure or every possible evolution. A hypothesis about a measured global sign should not be presented as a universal proof.
How would you state it in one sentence without making it sound established?
We hypothesize that, on unseen meshes, learned fluxes will produce density L1 error within 5% of the baseline and zero positive global entropy residuals.

To evaluate the hypothesis, the activity is to run a 1,000-step periodic EulerShockMesh-v1 comparison on unseen meshes against entropy-stable finite volumes, recording density L1, positive global entropy residuals, and conservation drift.

That specifies a proposed run and the quantities to record; it does not report that the run has happened. The comparison is on unseen meshes, extends for 1,000 periodic timesteps, and uses entropy-stable finite volumes as the baseline. The records cover the density-accuracy comparison, the sign of global entropy residuals, and conservation drift.
Does “EulerShockMesh-v1” tell us the mesh geometries or initial states?

Not from this statement alone. It names the setting for the activity, but does not describe its mesh geometries, initial states, or particular shock cases. We can keep that name without inferring specifications that have not been supplied.
Are the unseen meshes essential to the run, or could the comparison use only meshes the learned fluxes have seen?

Unseen meshes are explicit in the activity. A comparison confined to meshes already seen by the learned fluxes would not be this stated evaluation. The activity does not, however, define how the meshes are designated unseen or how many will be included.
What does the entropy-stable finite-volume method serve as here?

It is the comparison baseline for the run. Recording density L1 for the learned approach and for the entropy-stable finite volumes would make the hypothesized within-5% comparison interpretable, provided the errors are defined consistently. The activity does not give measured errors or say that either method has already satisfied a target.
Does “against entropy-stable finite volumes” mean their computed solution is automatically the reference used to define density L1 error?

No. A comparison baseline and an error reference are distinct concepts. The activity identifies the finite-volume baseline but does not specify the reference density field or the conventions used to calculate L1 error. We should not assume that the baseline solution itself is the error reference.
Then why record density L1 rather than just look at the two density fields?

Density L1 is the named accuracy quantity in the activity and in the hypothesis it is intended to evaluate. It provides a stated basis for comparing errors, whereas an informal visual comparison would not establish whether the learned fluxes are within 5% of the baseline’s error. The precise L1 calculation still needs a consistent definition before numerical values can be interpreted.
Are we measuring shock-position error in this run?

Not as a separately named record. Density L1 may reflect discrepancies around a shock, but it does not by itself report shock position. The activity lists density L1, positive global entropy residuals, and conservation drift; it does not specify a shock-position metric.
For the entropy record, is the important distinction positive versus nonpositive?

Yes. “Positive global entropy residuals” directs attention to occurrences with a positive sign under the chosen residual definition. Recording that quantity can address the hypothesis of zero positive global entropy residuals. The activity does not give the residual formula, its sign convention, or a numerical tolerance for deciding when a value is positive.
Should I interpret “record positive global entropy residuals” as requiring every residual to equal zero?

No. A record of positive residuals concerns whether positive values occur; a nonpositive value need not be exactly zero. Keeping those ideas separate matters because the hypothesis predicts zero *positive* global entropy residuals, not zero-valued residuals throughout the run.
Does a global entropy record tell us what happened at each individual face?

Not necessarily. A global residual is an aggregate assessment, and the activity does not separately call for face-level or cell-level entropy records. Even a run with no positive global residuals would not, solely on that basis, establish the sign of every local contribution.
What do we mean by conservation drift in the list of records?

In the context of the stated goal, conservation drift concerns mass, momentum, and energy over the evolution. Recording it alongside density L1 and entropy residuals keeps the conservation question visible during the 1,000-step run. The activity itself does not specify the normalization, the handling of momentum components, or whether a reported drift is the largest over the run or a value at a particular timestep.
Does this activity automatically test the below-10⁻⁶ normalized drift target from the goal?

It records conservation drift over 1,000 periodic steps, which is relevant to that target. But the target is specifically below 10⁻⁶ for normalized mass, momentum, and energy drift over 1,000 periodic, unforced timesteps. This activity says “periodic” but does not explicitly say “unforced,” and it does not define how drift is normalized. We should not claim the full target has been tested—or met—from the activity’s wording alone.
So periodic does not, by itself, mean unforced?

Correct. “Periodic” describes the stated setting of the run, while “unforced” would say something additional about forcing. The activity specifies the former and does not explicitly specify the latter. Neither a forcing condition nor a conservation result should be inferred just from the word “periodic.”
Is 1,000 steps a required duration for this activity, rather than a suggestion to stop whenever an interesting shock appears?

Yes. The activity says to run 1,000 steps. A shorter observation could be informative, but it would not be the full 1,000-step activity as stated. The wording does not specify a timestep size or a physical end time, so those should not be supplied as though fixed.
Do we need to say that the density L1 and entropy records are collected on unseen meshes, not merely that training happened elsewhere?

Yes. “On unseen meshes” qualifies the proposed run against the baseline. The resulting density L1, positive global entropy residuals, and conservation drift are to be recorded for that evaluation setting. The statement does not describe training or provide an unseen-mesh selection procedure.
Could I combine density L1, entropy residuals, and drift into one pass-or-fail score?

The activity calls for recording three distinct kinds of information, not combining them into a single score. Keeping them distinct lets the density comparison, entropy sign, and conservation behavior each be read on its own terms. A composite score could obscure a positive global entropy residual or substantial drift even if density L1 looked favorable; no composite scoring rule is stated here.
If the learned density L1 error is within 5% of the baseline, would that alone confirm the hypothesis?

No. It would address the hypothesis’s density L1 clause only, assuming the comparison is consistently defined on unseen meshes. The hypothesis also predicts zero positive global entropy residuals. Conservation drift is an additional record requested by the activity, even though it is not one of that hypothesis’s two stated predictions.
And if we record no positive global entropy residuals, can we conclude that the limiter specifically prevented them?

Not from this comparison alone. Such a record would speak to the observed global residuals for the evaluated evolution. It would not isolate the timestep entropy limiter’s causal contribution from the learned face dissipation or other aspects of the proposed construction. The activity specifies a comparison and records, not a component-isolation experiment.
Would an entropy-stable label on the finite-volume baseline make it unnecessary to record the baseline’s behavior?

The label identifies the baseline, but it is not a substitute for the comparison data needed to interpret the run. In particular, the within-5% density L1 hypothesis requires a baseline density L1 error measured under a consistent definition. The activity does not provide baseline results in advance.
Can the run establish that shocks are accurate on every possible unseen mesh?

No. It calls for an evaluation on unseen meshes, but does not specify a universal set of meshes. Its records can describe the meshes actually evaluated under the stated comparison; they should not be extended to every possible mesh. Moreover, density L1 is the named accuracy record, not a complete description of all shock properties.
How can we state the activity plainly without implying that any outcomes have already been measured?

Run EulerShockMesh-v1 for 1,000 periodic steps on unseen meshes, compare the learned approach with entropy-stable finite volumes, and record density L1, positive global entropy residuals, and conservation drift. That states the activity and its intended records without claiming a density-error result, an entropy outcome, or a conservation result.

The EulerShockMesh-v1 results on unseen meshes are in: density L1 is 0.0214 for the learned approach versus 0.0210 for the entropy-stable finite-volume baseline, a +1.9% difference. There are zero positive global entropy residuals, and the maximum normalized drift is 3.2×10⁻⁸.

Those are favorable results for the stated hypothesis on the evaluated unseen meshes. The learned approach’s density L1 error is 1.9% higher than the baseline’s, which is within the hypothesized 5% margin, and the recorded count of positive global entropy residuals is zero. The maximum normalized drift is 3.2×10⁻⁸. These are observations from EulerShockMesh-v1, not a guarantee for every unseen mesh.
